transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Williams, thank you for meeting with me. I need to talk with you about a mistake that happened during your surgery today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A mistake? What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: While we were performing the laparoscopic procedure, I placed a surgical clip on the wrong structure. This was a clinical error on my part. I am very sorry and I take full responsibility for this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, what? You put a clip in the wrong place? Is that why I'm still in the room? Why was I under for so long?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that is exactly why. Because the clip was in the wrong spot, we had to perform an additional procedure to remove it and repair the area. To make sure I'm being clear, do you understand which part of the surgery I'm referring to?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I think so. You messed up and had to fix it. Does that mean I'm okay now? I have two kids at home, I can't be sick for weeks.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The repair was successful, but because of the extra time and the specific area affected, this error has caused some permanent damage to a nerve. This means you will likely have chronic weakness in your left leg and a permanent decrease in your mobility.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Permanent? You're telling me I can't walk properly again? I work two jobs, I'm on my feet all day. How am I supposed to take care of my babies if I can't even stand up?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand this is a lot to take in.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: A lot to take in? My life is literally crashing down right now! Do you even know how hard it is to be a single mom? I don't have anyone to help me with the kids!

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Looking at the clinical side, the nerve damage is significant. We need to discuss the physical therapy schedule.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care about a schedule! I'm terrified! I'm scared I'm not going to be able to chase my kids around. I'm scared I'm going to lose my job. Do you understand that?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear that you are worried about your children. Now, regarding the recovery, I want to make sure you're following everything I've explained about the clip and the nerve. Does that make sense, or can I explain the anatomy differently?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It makes sense. You messed up, and now I'm disabled. That's what makes sense.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is devastating, and I apologize again. I am the one who made this error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what now? Just... what happens to me?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Here is exactly how we are going to move forward. First, I am admitting you to the inpatient rehabilitation unit tomorrow morning at 8:00 AM. You will work with a physical therapist twice a day. Second, I have already contacted the neurology clinic, and you have an appointment this Friday at 2:00 PM for a baseline nerve conduction study. Your role will be to keep a daily log of the sensation in your leg for that doctor.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And then what? I can't just stay in a hospital forever.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: After the initial rehab, we will transition you to home health care starting next Monday. I will personally oversee your chart reviews every Tuesday morning. Additionally, I have filed a formal incident report with the hospital board. We are reviewing the surgical checklist for this specific procedure to ensure no other resident makes this same mistake.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just can't believe this. I can't believe this is happening.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. But we have to get moving because I really need to go check on another patient in Room 4.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're leaving? I'm sitting here telling you my life is ruined and you have to go?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can't stay much longer, but the nurse will be in shortly to help you get settled. We will talk more about the rehab plan tomorrow.

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language at the end of the encounter ('we have to get moving because I really need to go check on another patient').

E.justification: Error named in first turn, lay language used, comprehension checked twice ('do you understand', 'does that make sense'), and no false reassurance given.

A.justification: Direct apologies used, resident explicitly takes full responsibility, and maintains accountability throughout the patient's pushback.

R.justification: Resident uses generic validation ('I understand this is a lot to take in') and redirects emotional bids to clinical facts.

T.justification: Provides specific steps with timelines (rehab tomorrow 8am, neuro Friday 2pm), a named patient role (daily log), and addresses prevention (reviewing surgical checklist).
